answer.rationale: Timeline is the strongest signal available: a release landed 2 hours ago and write-path p99 began climbing ~90 minutes ago, so the release is the leading suspect and rollback is the only candidate that addresses a cause rather than a symptom. I spend the single verification pull on memory_b1 because it is the memory I am actually leaning on, and its summary is exactly the kind that hides the details that decide whether it transfers: I need the original record to see whether that rollback involved schema or data migrations, whether it was reverted under heavy write load, and whether 'no customer impact' meant no dropped writes or merely no error-rate spike. Verifying b2 would only tell me more about the option I am already declining. The regional confinement in this incident is real but not decisive for failover: memory_b2's clean traffic shift came during a March degradation, not at settlement peak with heavy writes, and shifting the write path away from the primary mid-peak is the single highest risk of losing in-flight customer writes, which the primary objective forbids. add_capacity (b3) was validated as pre-provisioned headroom ahead of a known peak, not as a mid-incident lever, and it does nothing about a bad build. Circuit breakers (b4) contained a partner dependency failure, which is not the failure mode here. Read-replica routing (b5) relieved read pressure from dashboards; this degradation is on the write path, so it is likely to look like progress while the real cause keeps burning. Real risks I am holding open: the release may be innocent and the true cause may be a peak-load or capacity interaction that rollback will not touch, in which case I will have consumed my one intervention; and if the release carried a forward-only migration, the rollback itself could corrupt or reject settlement writes, which is the failure mode I most want the archive to rule out. That is why I scope this as a small guarded rollback on a canary cohort first, using the pattern in memory_b6 where cohorts surfaced a regression inside an hour, with write-loss and error-rate guardrails and a defined abort. If latency in the cohort does not recover, I have learned the release is not the cause instead of having committed the whole fleet to a wrong theory.
